entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Adolf of the Mark (1334–1347) was Prince-Bishop of Liège from 1313 to 1344, one of the longest and most turbulent episcopates in that powerful principality's history. The Prince-Bishops of Liège were among the most powerful ecclesiastical princes in the Low Countries, governing a wealthy industrial and commercial territory in the Meuse valley that included significant coal, metal-working, and textile industries — making Liège one of the wealthiest principalities in medieval northwestern Europe.

Adolf's long episcopate was marked by continuous conflict with the commune of Liège — one of the most politically assertive urban communities in northern Europe. The city of Liège's craft guilds and merchant class repeatedly challenged episcopal authority, asserting their rights and autonomy in a series of confrontations that foreshadowed the dramatic urban revolts of the fourteenth century. This tension between episcopal lordship and urban communal power was one of the defining dynamics of the medieval Liège principality.

The Mark family — from the County of Mark in Westphalia — used the Liège bishopric as a platform for their dynastic ambitions across the lower Rhine and Meuse regions. Adolf's tenure represented the family's decades-long hold on one of northern Europe's richest ecclesiastical prizes, and his management of the principality's complex political and economic affairs shaped the region's development.
